titleStmt.title: A theoretical review of consumer priming: Prospective theory, retrospective theory, and the affective–behavioral–cognitive model
titleStmt.author: Minton
Cornwell
Kahle

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: A theoretical review of consumer priming: Prospective theory, retrospective theory, and the affective–behavioral–cognitive model

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: method
span.quote: We add to this work by providing researchers a means for thinking about and constructing research on priming.

span.label: consumer priming
span.quote: Priming techniques are frequently used in marketing, advertising, and consumer behavior research but a holistic understanding of these techniques, measurement challenges, and theoretical foundations is not found in the literature.

span.label: review
span.quote: In the discussion to follow, the most common methods of priming in both psychology and marketing are reviewed, thereby fulfilling a call by Janiszewski and Wyer (2014) to identify ways to influence what is being primed.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Following a primed procedure consumes cognitive resources, which keeps the primed representation active and slows its decay relative to a declarative prime.
span.quote: Because greater cognitive resources are devoted to following the procedure, decay of procedural primes is much slower than primes involving declarative knowledge, and this is borne out in many empirical findings.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Uncertainty about a stimulus makes the consumer recruit the prime together with existing memory to resolve that uncertainty, which produces assimilation.
span.quote: In other words, assimilation effects are greatest when there is uncertainty surrounding a stimulus, and therefore, the prime is used with existing knowledge in memory to solve the uncertainty.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: High motivation raises processing depth, which triggers correction of the judgment for the perceived persuasion attempt and so flips assimilation into contrast.
span.quote: When motivation is high, processing is higher, leading to correction in judgments to account for persuasion.

span.label: The paper deliberately excludes the content-versus-process priming distinctions covered by the prior review it builds on, so its coverage of priming distinctions is partial by design.
span.quote: Specific distinctions made by Janiszewski and Wyer (2014), such as the nuances distinguishing content versus process priming, are not further discussed here in order to focus on new contributions.

span.label: The framework's central measurement-discrepancy proposal is asserted rather than empirically tested, and the authors state it still needs testing.
span.quote: There is a great need for further testing of measurement discrepancy issues to identify if measurement similarity provides new and more accurate insight into consumer behavior.

span.label: The tri-component ABC model of attitudes is imported as the organizing scheme for a marketing/consumer-behaviour priming framework.
span.quote: In developing the priming framework, each type of prime is categorized by priming outcome: affective, behavioral, and cognitive, which follows suit with the tri-component ABC model of attitudes (Breckler, 1984).

span.label: priming
span.quote: It describes priming as an improvement in performance, priming can also involve a change in performance that is neutral or results in poorer performance, as will be evidenced in a later discussion on reactant priming responses

span.label: prime
span.quote: Some researchers also refer to the prime as the stimulus or independent variable; however, a stimulus or an independent variable is only a prime if it increases knowledge activation that influences response to a target

span.label: knowledge activation
span.quote: Within the priming paradigm, the prime is the item used to manipulate or increase knowledge activation, and the target is what the prime is applied to in an effort to produce specific outcomes

span.label: target
span.quote: Within the priming paradigm, the prime is the item used to manipulate or increase knowledge activation, and the target is what the prime is applied to in an effort to produce specific outcomes

span.label: ABC model
span.quote: In developing the priming framework, each type of prime is categorized by priming outcome: affective, behavioral, and cognitive, which follows suit with the tri-component ABC model of attitudes

span.label: spreading activation theory
span.quote: Most marketing research cites spreading activation theory as the underlying process model of priming, without adequate attention to other theories of priming

span.label: A DEFINITION QUOTED AND THEN CORRECTED IN THE SAME PAGE, which is exactly what this corpus is for. McNamara (2005) is quoted verbatim - priming is `an IMPROVEMENT in performance in a perceptual or cognitive task, relative to an appropriate baseline, produced by context or prior experience` - and then: `while McNamara (2005) describes priming as an improvement in performance, PRIMING CAN ALSO INVOLVE A CHANGE IN PERFORMANCE THAT IS NEUTRAL OR RESULTS IN POORER PERFORMANCE.` The correction is not a rival definition; it strikes one word out of the standard one, and it does so because reactant priming exists
span.quote: It describes priming as an improvement in performance, priming can also involve a change in performance that is neutral or results in poorer performance, as will be evidenced in a later discussion on reactant priming responses

span.label: A NECESSARY CONDITION FOR BEING A PRIME, WHICH IS RARER THAN A DEFINITION: `Some researchers also refer to the prime as the stimulus or independent variable; HOWEVER, A STIMULUS OR AN INDEPENDENT VARIABLE IS ONLY A PRIME IF IT INCREASES KNOWLEDGE ACTIVATION that influences response to a target.` This says which manipulations are EXCLUDED, and it draws the boundary with a mechanism rather than with a procedure - so whether something is a prime is not settled by how it was presented or by what it looked like, but by what it did to activation
span.quote: Some researchers also refer to the prime as the stimulus or independent variable; however, a stimulus or an independent variable is only a prime if it increases knowledge activation that influences response to a target

span.label: THE TAXONOMY IS IMPORTED FROM ATTITUDE THEORY, NOT DERIVED FROM PRIMING RESEARCH: priming is sorted by OUTCOME into affective, behavioral and cognitive, `WHICH FOLLOWS SUIT WITH THE TRI-COMPONENT ABC MODEL OF ATTITUDES (Breckler, 1984)`. Sorting by outcome rather than by method is the substantive choice - two techniques that look nothing alike land in the same box if they move the same thing, and one technique can appear twice. The paper is explicit that this is a borrowing, which is what makes it checkable against the source literature
span.quote: In developing the priming framework, each type of prime is categorized by priming outcome: affective, behavioral, and cognitive, which follows suit with the tri-component ABC model of attitudes

span.label: THE COMPLAINT THAT MOTIVATES THE WHOLE REVIEW IS MONOCULTURE, NOT ERROR: `MOST MARKETING RESEARCH CITES SPREADING ACTIVATION THEORY as the underlying process model of priming, WITHOUT ADEQUATE ATTENTION TO OTHER THEORIES of priming.` Nobody is said to be wrong. The charge is that one account is cited by default, so its alternatives are never tested against it - and the paper's answer is to review prospective and retrospective memory models alongside it rather than to replace it
span.quote: Most marketing research cites spreading activation theory as the underlying process model of priming, without adequate attention to other theories of priming

span.label: extends → Janiszewski and Wyer (2014) review of priming in marketing
span.quote: This holistic priming framework extends Janiszewski and Wyer’s (2014) priming review to show the importance of priming limitations, especially in relation to survey research (i.e., measurement discrepancy).

span.label: builds-on → Breckler (1984) tri-component (ABC) model of attitudes
span.quote: The offered framework has benefited from the review of priming by Janiszewski and Wyer (2014) and the theorizing of the tri-component model (Breckler, 1984).

span.label: prime —causes→ knowledge activation
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.95 — THIS EDGE IS DEFINITIONAL, NOT EMPIRICAL, AND THAT IS WHY IT IS WEIGHTED 0.95. The paper is not reporting that primes raise activation; it is saying that a thing which does not raise activation IS NOT A PRIME. The direction is inside the quote and cannot be read the other way.
span.quote: Some researchers also refer to the prime as the stimulus or independent variable; however, a stimulus or an independent variable is only a prime if it increases knowledge activation that influences response to a target

span.label: prime —distinct-from→ target
span.note: differs in: WHICH SIDE OF THE MANIPULATION EACH IS ON. The prime is what raises activation; the target is what the prime is applied to and where the outcome is measured. The two definitions are mutually referring - neither can be stated without the other - so this is a distinction internal to one paradigm rather than between two things that exist independently · strength of the relation: 0.9 — Both halves of the definition are in the one span, which is the point: the paper defines them together in a single sentence.
span.quote: Within the priming paradigm, the prime is the item used to manipulate or increase knowledge activation, and the target is what the prime is applied to in an effort to produce specific outcomes

span.label: ABC model —operationalised-as→ priming
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.85 — THE DIRECTION IS THE UNUSUAL PART: an ATTITUDE model is being used to operationalise a MEMORY phenomenon. Weighted 0.85 because the paper asserts the correspondence (`follows suit with`) rather than arguing for it - the three attitude components are taken as the right three boxes for priming outcomes without a test that they are exhaustive or exclusive.
span.quote: In developing the priming framework, each type of prime is categorized by priming outcome: affective, behavioral, and cognitive, which follows suit with the tri-component ABC model of attitudes

span.label: The review sorts every priming technique into three outcome classes - affective, behavioral and cognitive - borrowed from the tri-component ABC model of attitudes.
span.quote: In developing the priming framework, each type of prime is categorized by priming outcome: affective, behavioral, and cognitive, which follows suit with the tri-component ABC model of attitudes (Breckler, 1984).

span.label: Priming theories are grouped into two prospective theories - spreading activation and expectancy - and two retrospective theories - semantic matching and compound-cue.
span.quote: There are two main prospective priming theories: (i) spreading activation theory and (ii) expectancy theory, as well as two main retrospective priming theories: (i) semantic matching theory and (ii) compound-cue theory.

span.label: Compound cue theory and spreading activation theory cannot be combined into one account because they rest on incompatible underlying models of memory.
span.quote: Thus, while some theories may be able to work together as Neely and Keefe (1989) describe, compound cue theory and spreading activation, in particular, are in direct opposition to one another because of their foundation in different models of memory.

span.label: Prospective and retrospective theories differ only in process; both converge on the same endpoint of increased knowledge activation.
span.quote: Both prospective and retrospective theories lead to the same end result of increased knowledge activation.

span.label: A stimulus or independent variable counts as a prime only when it raises knowledge activation that then shapes the response to a target.
span.quote: Some researchers also refer to the prime as the stimulus or independent variable; however, a stimulus or an independent variable is only a prime if it increases knowledge activation that influences response to a target.

span.label: The commonest measurement discrepancy in survey-based priming work is priming behavior but measuring the effect with cognitive purchase-intention questions.
span.quote: One of the most common discrepancies occurs when researchers create surveys that use behavioral priming methods to encourage a consumer to purchase a product, yet measure the effects of priming through cognitive-based purchase intention questions.

span.label: Consumers respond to a prime either consistently with it or reactantly against it, and the paper attributes the reactant (contrast) case to consumer traits and states such as skepticism and concern about persuasion rather than to processing nodes alone.
span.quote: We argue that reactance (i.e., apparent contrast effects) may stem from trait and state variables such as a consumer’s tendency toward skepticism or manipulation of their concern for persuasion.

span.label: Procedural primes persist far longer than declarative primes, whose activation typically decays within seconds.
span.quote: Because greater cognitive resources are devoted to following the procedure, decay of procedural primes is much slower than primes involving declarative knowledge, and this is borne out in many empirical findings.

span.label: priming
span.quote: McNamara (2005) defines priming as “an improvement in performance in a perceptual or cognitive task, relative to an appropriate baseline, produced by context or prior experience” (p. 3).

span.label: prime and target
span.quote: Within the priming paradigm, the prime is the item used to manipulate or increase knowledge activation, and the target is what the prime is applied to in an effort to produce specific outcomes (Higgins et al., 1985).

span.label: behavioral priming
span.quote: Behavioral priming, sometimes also referred to as social priming, results in increased participation in prime-activated behaviors.

span.label: procedural priming
span.quote: Procedural priming falls under the umbrella of behavioral priming but focuses specifically on priming a process, such as strategies or methods for processing information.

span.label: goal priming
span.quote: Goal priming, another type of behavioral priming, focuses on activation of end-goal states thereby leading individuals to behave in ways consistent with goal attainment (Forster et al., 2009).

span.label: cognitive priming
span.quote: Cognitive priming refers to changes in thought based upon the presence of a prime (Myers and Hansen, 2012).

span.label: category priming
span.quote: Category priming is a type of cognitive priming that occurs when a subset of terms (e.g., high class) is primed thereby influencing response to a target.

span.label: semantic priming
span.quote: Semantic priming, another form of cognitive priming, considers how a word, phrase, sign, or symbol can influence response to a stimulus.

span.label: associative priming
span.quote: Semantic priming occurs as a result of direct semantic relation between words (e.g., bronze is a type of gold), whereas associative priming occurs because of common relations developed in the mind that are not necessarily semantically related (e.g., dogs are associated with bones).

span.label: associative boost
span.quote: Moss et al. (1995) note that priming studies can feature both associative and semantic elements resulting in greater effect sizes through what is called an associative boost.

span.label: conceptual versus perceptual priming
span.quote: As McNamara and Holbrook (2003) describe, conceptual priming focuses on meaning, while perceptual priming focuses on the form of the stimulus.

span.label: repetition priming
span.quote: Simple repetition priming is described by Eysenck (2004) as the “more efficient processing of a stimulus when it has been presented and processed previously” (p. 313).

span.label: contextual priming
span.quote: Contextual priming, also known as environmental cueing, has been defined in communications as manipulation or activation of knowledge using marketing cues that precede or surround a target advertisement (Yi, 1990a, 1990b).

span.label: masked priming
span.quote: In contrast to priming techniques that allow seconds, minutes, or even longer between presentation of the prime and the target, masked priming shows a prime for a short time (sometimes just 50–60 ms) with a target immediately following the prime (Kinoshita and Lupker, 2003).

span.label: spreading activation theory
span.quote: Spreading activation theory states that a prime activates nodes in memory that are associated with the prime (Quillian, 1967).

span.label: expectancy theory
span.quote: In contrast to spreading activation theory, expectancy theory posits that upon exposure to a prime, one’s mind automatically creates a set of expected targets, often words (Posner and Snyder, 1975).

span.label: semantic matching theory
span.quote: Turning to retrospective theories, semantic matching theory states that individuals are exposed to both the prime and target and then use the prime to make sense of the target (Neely and Keefe, 1989).

span.label: compound cue theory
span.quote: Once presented with the prime and target, this compound cue in short-term memory is matched to compounds already existing in long-term memory (Ratcliff and McKoon, 1988).

span.label: prospective theories of priming
span.quote: Prospective theories of priming describe a prime as activating knowledge, which then influences response to a target; thus, the majority of the priming process occurs before exposure to the target.

span.label: priming method (as distinct from priming technique)
span.term: priming method (as distinct from priming technique)
span.quote: Priming techniques can be partnered with a priming method (e.g., conceptual, perceptual, repetition, or contextual priming) to produce a priming outcome.

span.label: 0.49 versus 0.25 — Average effect size of associative priming studies compared with semantic priming studies, as reported in the meta-review the paper cites
span.quote: In a meta-review of semantic priming studies, Lucas (2000) found that associative priming studies resulted in greater effect sizes (average of 0.49) in comparison with semantic priming studies (average of 0.25).

span.label: 0.26 — Size of the increase in priming effects attributed to the associative boost (a prime that is both semantically and associatively related)
span.quote: Lucas (2000) also shows that the associative boost (i.e., both semantic and associative relationships) increases priming effects by 0.26.
